start.title: Start here: your Helm 2 path
start.description: You already know what Helm does if you took the Helm 3 course: a chart plus values becomes a release. Helm 2 does the same job with one extra moving part,…
start.html:
You already know what Helm does if you took the Helm 3 course: a chart plus values becomes a release. Helm 2 does the same job with one extra moving part, and that part changes how you install, how you clean up, and how you stay safe.

The big idea
Helm 2 is two programs. The helm2 client on your computer, and Tiller, a server that runs inside the cluster. The client sends charts to Tiller; Tiller talks to Kubernetes and remembers every release.

Why Helm 2 still matters

Helm 2 reached the end of its support in November 2020. You will still meet it:

  • in older clusters whose upgrade never happened,
  • in scripts and CI jobs written before Helm 3,
  • and in the KubeDojo playground, which simulates Helm 2 with Tiller (its guide section 9 · Helm 2 + Tiller).

On a machine that has both versions, Helm 2 is usually installed as helm2 and Helm 3 as helm. This course follows that habit, like the playground does.

What you will be able to do

  1. Install Tiller and check that both halves match.
  2. Install a release with --name, then upgrade it, break it, and roll it back.
  3. Delete a release, and understand why --purge matters.
  4. Explain why Tiller was a security risk, and move releases to Helm 3.
Remember
  • Helm 2 = the helm2 client + Tiller in the cluster.
  • Charts, values, and releases mean the same as in Helm 3.
  • Use Simulate any time to practise without a cluster.

options: Older clusters and charts still use it, and the KubeDojo playground runs it
quiz.why: Helm 2 stopped getting updates in November 2020, but plenty of clusters, scripts, and charts still expect it.

quiz.q: What is the biggest difference between Helm 2 and Helm 3?
options: Helm 2 needs Tiller, a server running inside the cluster
quiz.why: Helm 3 removed Tiller. Everything else (charts, values, releases) carries over.

tiller.title: Tiller: the server Helm 2 needs
tiller.description: You type helm2 install and get Error: could not find tiller. Your chart is fine. Helm 2 just has nobody in the cluster to send it to. Tiller is Helm 2’s…
tiller.html:
The problem
You type helm2 install and get Error: could not find tiller. Your chart is fine. Helm 2 just has nobody in the cluster to send it to.
The big idea
Tiller is Helm 2’s server. helm2 init installs it into the cluster as the tiller-deploy Deployment in kube-system. From then on, the client sends every install, upgrade, and rollback to Tiller, and Tiller stores each release revision as a ConfigMap next to it.

Install Tiller

Tiller acts on the cluster with the permissions of its own service account, so create one first:

kubectl -n kube-system create serviceaccount tiller
kubectl create clusterrolebinding tiller --clusterrole=cluster-admin --serviceaccount=kube-system:tiller
helm2 init --service-account tiller --wait

Then check both halves:

kubectl -n kube-system get deploy tiller-deploy
helm2 version --short

helm2 version prints a Client and a Server line. If the server line is missing, Tiller is not reachable; if the versions differ, run helm2 init --upgrade.

Think of it like…
A shop counter. You (the client) hand an order (the chart) over the counter; the clerk behind it (Tiller) does the work in the back room and files the receipt (the release history).
The cluster-admin binding above is the quick, common setup, and the reason Tiller was risky: anything that can talk to Tiller can do anything in the cluster. Lesson 6 shows how teams locked it down.
Remember
  • helm2 init installs Tiller into kube-system.
  • Tiller works with its own service account’s permissions.
  • helm2 version shows both halves; they should match.

options: On your laptop, next to the helm2 client
Inside the cluster, usually as the tiller-deploy Deployment in kube-system
In a cloud service run by the Helm project
quiz.why: helm2 init installs Tiller into the cluster. The client finds it there.

quiz.q: You run helm2 ls and see "Error could not find tiller". What is missing?
options: Tiller has not been installed in this cluster yet
quiz.why: Every Helm 2 command that touches releases goes through Tiller, so install it first with helm2 init.

install.title: Install a release with --name
install.description: In Helm 2 the release name is a flag: helm2 install./pizza-chart --name pizza. Leave it out and Tiller makes one up, which is hard to find again. Always…
install.html:
The big idea
In Helm 2 the release name is a flag: helm2 install ./pizza-chart --name pizza. Leave it out and Tiller makes one up, which is hard to find again. Always name your releases.

Install, wait, and look

helm2 install ./pizza-chart --name pizza --namespace helm-practice --wait --timeout 120
helm2 ls
helm2 status pizza
  • --wait keeps the command running until the Pods are ready, like in Helm 3.
  • --timeout is a number of seconds in Helm 2 (Helm 3 uses durations such as 2m).
  • helm2 ls shows the release as DEPLOYED, in capital letters.

Try it before using a terminal

Install Tiller first, then the release, and use Next step to follow the handoff from Tiller to Kubernetes.

Remember
  • Name every release with --name.
  • --timeout counts seconds in Helm 2.
  • helm2 ls asks Tiller what is installed.

quiz.q: You run helm2 install ./pizza-chart without --name. What happens?
options: Tiller invents a release name, such as wandering-otter
quiz.why: In Helm 2 the name is optional and random by default. Helm 3 made it required.

quiz.q: Which command lists the releases Tiller knows about?
quiz.why: helm2 ls (or helm2 list) asks Tiller for its releases.

upgrade.title: Upgrade, break, and roll back
upgrade.description: You upgrade to three copies of a new version. Then someone ships an image tag that does not exist. The app must keep serving while you put it back. Tiller…
upgrade.html:
The problem
You upgrade to three copies of a new version. Then someone ships an image tag that does not exist. The app must keep serving while you put it back.
helm2 upgrade pizza ./pizza-chart --set replicaCount=3 --set image.tag=1.28 --wait --timeout 120
helm2 upgrade pizza ./pizza-chart --set replicaCount=3 --set image.tag=does-not-exist --wait --timeout 120
helm2 history pizza
helm2 rollback pizza 2 --wait
The big idea
Tiller keeps every revision. helm2 history shows them; helm2 rollback NAME REVISION reapplies an old one as a new revision. When you pass --set or -f, helm2 upgrade starts again from the chart’s defaults plus what you passed, so earlier settings you did not repeat are dropped. Add --reuse-values to keep them.

Practise it

Install, upgrade to three copies, try the missing image, then roll back to the revision that worked.

Remember
  • Failed revisions are recorded, and the old Pods can keep serving.
  • rollback creates a new revision.
  • Use --reuse-values when you mean “change only this”.

quiz.q: An upgrade used an image that does not exist. The old Pods keep serving. What does helm2 history pizza show for the new revision?
options: Nothing; failed upgrades are not recorded
quiz.why: Tiller records the failed revision. That history is what lets you roll back with confidence.

quiz.q: After helm2 rollback pizza 2, which revision number does the release have?
options: A new, higher number that reuses revision 2’s settings
quiz.why: A rollback is a new revision. History only ever grows.

delete.title: Delete, and purge the history
delete.description: helm2 delete pizza removes the app’s Kubernetes objects but keeps the release history in Tiller. The name stays taken, and you could even roll the deleted…
delete.html:
The big idea
helm2 delete pizza removes the app’s Kubernetes objects but keeps the release history in Tiller. The name stays taken, and you could even roll the deleted release back. helm2 delete --purge pizza removes the history too. Helm 3’s uninstall behaves like --purge by default.
helm2 delete pizza
helm2 ls --deleted
helm2 delete --purge pizza
Purging is final: the history and the ability to roll back are gone. Charts can also leave things behind on purpose, such as PersistentVolumeClaims. Check with kubectl get pvc -n helm-practice.
Remember
  • delete keeps history; delete --purge frees the name.
  • helm2 ls --deleted shows what is still remembered.
  • Helm 3 uninstall purges by default.

quiz.q: You ran helm2 delete pizza and now helm2 install --name pizza fails with “cannot re-use a name”. Why?
options: Tiller still keeps the deleted release’s history, so the name is taken
Release names can only be used once per cluster, forever
quiz.why: helm2 delete keeps the history. helm2 delete --purge removes it and frees the name.

quiz.q: Which command shows releases that were deleted but not purged?
quiz.why: Deleted releases are hidden from a plain helm2 ls.

security.title: Tiller’s power, and how teams locked it down
security.description: A developer with read-only access to one namespace runs helm2 install and creates objects everywhere. Their RBAC said no; Tiller, running as cluster-admin,…
security.html:
The problem
A developer with read-only access to one namespace runs helm2 install and creates objects everywhere. Their RBAC said no; Tiller, running as cluster-admin, said yes.
The big idea
Tiller acts with its own service account’s permissions, not yours. With the common cluster-admin setup, anything that can reach Tiller’s port (44134) can change anything in the cluster.

How teams locked it down

  • One Tiller per team namespace, each with a service account limited to that namespace: helm2 init --tiller-namespace team-a --service-account tiller, and clients use --tiller-namespace team-a.
  • TLS between client and Tiller, so only holders of a certificate can talk to it: helm2 init --tiller-tls --tiller-tls-verify ....
  • Keep history small: helm2 init --history-max 200 stops thousands of ConfigMaps piling up in kube-system.
Think of it like…
A master key hanging by the door. Convenient, until you notice that everyone who walks past can pick it up.
Remember
  • Tiller’s permissions, not yours, decide what an install can do.
  • Lock it down per namespace, with TLS, and with a history limit.
  • Helm 3 removed the problem by removing Tiller.

quiz.q: Why was a default Tiller a security problem?
options: Anyone who could reach Tiller could act with Tiller’s permissions, often cluster-admin
It stored charts in plain text
quiz.why: Tiller’s gRPC port had no authentication by default, so it bypassed the caller’s own RBAC.

quiz.q: How does Helm 3 avoid the problem?
options: It removed Tiller; the helm client acts with your own kubeconfig permissions
It runs Tiller on your laptop
quiz.why: Without a server in the cluster, Helm can only do what you are allowed to do.

migrate.title: Move to Helm 3 with helm-2to3
migrate.description: Moving to Helm 3 does not touch your running apps. The helm-2to3 plugin copies Helm 2’s settings and each release’s history into Helm 3’s format. Then Helm…
migrate.html:
The big idea
Moving to Helm 3 does not touch your running apps. The helm-2to3 plugin copies Helm 2’s settings and each release’s history into Helm 3’s format. Then Helm 3 manages them, and Tiller can go.
helm plugin install https://github.com/helm/helm-2to3
helm 2to3 move config
helm 2to3 convert pizza --dry-run
helm 2to3 convert pizza
helm ls -A
helm 2to3 cleanup
  1. move config copies repositories and plugins from Helm 2’s home to Helm 3’s.
  2. convert moves one release at a time; try --dry-run first. Afterwards helm ls -A (Helm 3) shows it.
  3. cleanup removes Tiller and the Helm 2 data. Run it last, once every release is converted.
Charts with apiVersion: v2 are Helm 3 only. Helm 3 still installs older apiVersion: v1 charts, and moves their requirements.yaml dependencies into Chart.yaml when you update them.
Remember
  • move config → convert each release → check → cleanup.
  • Converting does not restart your app.
  • Clean up last.

quiz.q: What does helm 2to3 convert pizza do?
options: Copies the release’s Helm 2 history into Helm 3’s format, so Helm 3 can manage it
Deletes the running Pods and reinstalls them
quiz.why: The app keeps running. Only Helm’s record of the release moves.

quiz.q: When should you run helm 2to3 cleanup?
options: Last, after every release is converted and checked with Helm 3
quiz.why: Cleanup removes Tiller and the Helm 2 data. Do it only when nothing needs Helm 2 any more.
